title: Books & Language Shorts · Episode 1
chapters: The dark origins of fairy tales
Invented languages: from Esperanto to Klingon

units.t: Books & Language Shorts. Episode one.
In this episode: Pen names: why writers hide, The dark origins of fairy tales and Invented languages: from Esperanto to Klingon.
Part one. Pen names: why writers hide.
George Orwell, Mark Twain and George Eliot were not real names.
Behind every pen name is a reason, from prejudice to privacy to a bit of mischief.
Not who they seemed.
A pen name, also called a pseudonym or nom de plume, is a name an author publishes under instead of their own.
The practice is ancient and widespread.
Voltaire was born François-Marie Arouet.
Lewis Carroll was Charles Dodgson.
George Orwell was Eric Arthur Blair.
Australian readers know Henry Handel Richardson, author of The Fortunes of Richard Mahony, but the writer was in fact Ethel Florence Lindesay Richardson.
Writers have adopted pen names to escape prejudice, to protect their families, to keep a day job, to separate different kinds of writing, or simply because they liked the sound of something better.
Each disguise tells a small story about the pressures writers faced in their time.
Bells and Eliot.
In 1846 three sisters in a Yorkshire parsonage published poems as Currer, Ellis and Acton Bell.
In 1847 Jane Eyre by Currer Bell became a sensation, and Wuthering Heights and Agnes Grey followed.
The authors were Charlotte, Emily and Anne Brontë.
They chose names that were not obviously female because, Charlotte later explained, critics treated women writers with prejudice.
Charlotte and Anne revealed themselves to their publisher in 1848.
Mary Ann Evans, a respected editor and translator, turned to fiction in the 1850s as George Eliot.
She wanted her work judged as serious literature, not light romance.
She also lived openly with the married writer George Henry Lewes, a scandal in Victorian England.
A male name kept attention on the books.
Her identity soon leaked, but she kept the name.
Twain and Orwell.
Samuel Clemens worked as a Mississippi riverboat pilot before he became a writer.
On the river, crew called out depth readings, and mark twain meant the second mark on the line: two fathoms, about 3.
7 metres, deep enough for a steamboat to pass safely.
Clemens began signing his newspaper writing Mark Twain in 1863.
Eric Blair adopted the name George Orwell in 1933 for his first book, Down and Out in Paris and London, partly to spare his family embarrassment about his time living in poverty.
George was a solidly English name, and the River Orwell in Suffolk was one he knew.
Both disguises became so famous that the real names now sound like the pseudonyms.
Starting over in secret.
Pen names are not only for beginners.
Stephen King published several novels as Richard Bachman, partly because publishers then believed more than about one book a year by the same author would saturate the market.
A bookshop worker noticed similarities and researched copyright records, and King was exposed in 1985.
J.
K.
Rowling's initials were themselves a kind of disguise.
Her publisher suggested boys might be reluctant to read a book by a woman, and she borrowed the K from her grandmother Kathleen.
In 2013 she published a crime novel, The Cuckoo's Calling, as Robert Galbraith.
It had modest sales until her authorship leaked, after which it shot up the bestseller lists overnight.
The Galbraith episode suggests that names strongly influence sales, if not quality.
The writer behind the curtain.
The Italian novelist who writes as Elena Ferrante has kept her real identity officially private since her first novel in 1992, even as her Neapolitan novels became international bestsellers.
She has said that books, once written, do not need their authors.
Journalists have tried to unmask her, prompting fierce debate about whether readers have any right to know.
Pen names raise interesting questions.
Does knowing an author's gender, background or reputation change how we read?
Today, pen names are also common in genre fiction, where authors may write romance under one name and thrillers under another so that loyal readers know what to expect.
The key idea: A pen name is an invented name an author publishes under, and writers have long used them for reasons from prejudice to privacy.
Part two. The dark origins of fairy tales.
Before Disney, Cinderella's stepsisters cut off parts of their feet to fit the slipper.
Fairy tales have a long, strange and sometimes gruesome history.
Older than writing.
Long before anyone wrote them down, fairy tales were told aloud, by grandparents at the fire, by workers passing the time and by nurses to children.
They were not just for kids.
Adults told tales of clever peasants, cruel stepmothers and magical helpers to entertain each other and pass on lessons.
Because the tales lived in memory, they changed with each teller and crossed borders.
Folklorists catalogue thousands of tale types in the Aarne-Thompson-Uther index.
Cinderella is a good example.
The Greek writer Strabo recorded the story of Rhodopis, whose sandal an eagle dropped in an Egyptian king's lap.
A 9th-century Chinese tale tells of Ye Xian, helped by a fish's bones, who loses a golden shoe.
Perrault and Basile.
In 1697, Charles Perrault, a member of the French Academy, published a small book of tales that included 'Cinderella', 'Sleeping Beauty', 'Little Red Riding Hood' and 'Puss in Boots'.
He polished folk tales for fashionable readers at the court of Louis XIV, adding wit and ending each tale with a little moral in verse.
Perrault gave us the pumpkin coach and the glass slipper.
His Red Riding Hood ends badly: the wolf eats her, and no woodcutter arrives.
The moral warns young women about smooth-talking men.
Earlier, in the 1630s, the Italian writer Giambattista Basile had published his own collection, including early versions of Cinderella and Sleeping Beauty.
The Brothers Grimm.
In 1812, the German scholars Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm published the first volume of their Children's and Household Tales.
They were language experts who wanted to preserve what they saw as the authentic voice of the German people, at a time when Germany was divided and occupied by Napoleon's France.
Their image of peasants telling ancient tales is a little misleading.
Many storytellers were educated, middle-class young women, some of French Huguenot descent, who already knew Perrault's tales.
One prized source, Dorothea Viehmann, was a tailor's widow with a vast memory for stories.
The brothers revised the collection repeatedly, and the final edition of 1857 held around 200 tales.
Softer, but bloodier.
The first Grimm edition was not a children's book, and parents complained.
So Wilhelm in particular reworked the tales for family reading.
Sexual hints went.
In the first 'Rapunzel', the witch discovers the prince's visits when Rapunzel innocently remarks that her clothes are getting tight around her waist.
Later editions changed this to a harmless slip of the tongue.
Evil mothers were often turned into stepmothers, to protect the ideal of motherhood.
Violence mostly stayed, because it punished wickedness.
In the Grimms' Cinderella, the stepsisters cut off a toe and a heel to fit the slipper, and at the wedding, birds peck out their eyes.
Andersen and endurance.
Hans Christian Andersen mostly invented new tales, starting in 1835: 'The Little Mermaid', 'The Ugly Duckling', 'The Emperor's New Clothes' and 'The Snow Queen'.
In his original 'Little Mermaid', the prince marries someone else.
She refuses to kill him to save herself and dissolves into foam, becoming a spirit of the air.
Many readers see Andersen's own loneliness in his stories.
Fairy tales keep returning because they deal with growing up, injustice, luck and courage.
In 1976 Bruno Bettelheim argued that their frightening parts help children face fears safely, though his ideas are debated.
A 2016 study suggested some tales may be thousands of years old, though such estimates are uncertain.
The key idea: Fairy tales began as spoken folk tales, and Cinderella-type stories have been told around the world for well over a thousand years.
Part three. Invented languages: from Esperanto to Klingon.
People have built entire languages from scratch, hoping to unite the world, deepen a fantasy, or just for fun.
Most failed.
A few took on lives of their own.
A very old hobby.
Constructed languages, often called conlangs, are designed by a person rather than evolving naturally in a community.
One of the earliest recorded is the Lingua Ignota, or unknown language, created by the German abbess Hildegard of Bingen in the twelfth century, with around a thousand invented words.
In the 1600s, philosophers such as John Wilkins in England tried to build perfectly logical languages, where every word's form would reveal its meaning by sorting all of reality into categories.
These schemes were brilliant and unusable.
Historians have counted hundreds of attempts.
Their makers have had three main motives: to help people from different nations communicate, to explore ideas about logic and thought, or to bring a fictional world to life.
Volapük, then Esperanto.
In 1879 Johann Martin Schleyer, a Catholic priest in southern Germany, published Volapük, an international language.
In the 1880s it spread astonishingly fast, with clubs, journals and congresses, and supporters claimed a very large following, though such numbers are hard to verify.
But Volapük was difficult, with complex grammar and words so altered from their sources that they were hard to recognise.
When reformers proposed simplifying it, Schleyer insisted on keeping control, and the movement split.
Within a few years most followers had moved to a rival.
That rival was Esperanto, published in 1887 by Ludwik Zamenhof, an eye doctor from Białystok, then part of the Russian Empire.
He believed a neutral shared language could reduce the mistrust between the Poles, Jews, Germans and Russians around him.
Spelling is phonetic and grammar has very few exceptions.
Persecuted but persistent.
Esperanto's internationalism made authoritarian regimes suspicious.
In Nazi Germany it was attacked as a Jewish conspiracy, partly because Zamenhof was Jewish, and the movement was suppressed.
In Stalin's Soviet Union, many Esperantists were arrested in the purges of the late 1930s, accused of contact with foreigners.
Zamenhof's own children were killed in the Holocaust.
Even so, the language survived, holding world congresses, publishing original literature and translations, and later thriving online.
Estimates of speakers vary enormously, from tens of thousands of fluent users to perhaps a couple of million with some knowledge.
It never became the global second language its founder hoped for.
English largely took that role, for reasons of power and economics rather than design.
Still, it remains the most successful international language ever created.
Tolkien's secret vice.
J.
R.
R.
Tolkien was a professional philologist, an expert in the history of languages, and he invented languages from his teenage years onwards.
He called the hobby his secret vice in a 1931 lecture.
For Tolkien, the languages came before the stories.
He later explained that he built his mythology partly to give his languages a world and a history in which they could exist.
His two main Elvish languages were modelled on real ones he loved.
Quenya drew on the sounds of Finnish, while Sindarin was influenced by Welsh.
He also worked out how they had changed over thousands of years of imagined history.
That depth helps explain why Middle-earth feels so ancient: its names carry the weight of invented centuries.
Klingon and Dothraki.
In 1984 the linguist Marc Okrand developed the Klingon language for the film Star Trek III, building on a few words used earlier in the series.
He deliberately gave it unusual features to sound alien, including a basic word order of object, verb, subject, which is rare among human languages.
The Klingon Dictionary followed in 1985, and devoted fans have since translated works including Hamlet.
Later, the linguist David J.
Peterson created Dothraki and High Valyrian for the television series Game of Thrones, and languages for many other productions.
These languages have consistent grammar and vocabulary, which is why fans can learn them.
Some have even appeared in mainstream language learning apps, a sign of how seriously the art is now taken.
The key idea: People have invented languages for nearly nine centuries, for logic, communication or fiction.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. Why have writers adopted pen names?
Answer. To avoid prejudice or protect privacy.
Question two. Why do very similar fairy tales appear in many different countries?
Answer. Spoken tales changed with each teller and crossed borders.
Question three. What did philosophers like John Wilkins try to build?
Answer. Logical languages where words reveal meaning.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
